findings.problem: The section teaches the change of Manager of Record as an approval with no clock: 'No day count is stated in 247 CMR 6.10', table 0 labels it 'Prior Board approval needed? Yes', and retrieval_prompts[12] drills it as a change with no day count. It never mentions 247 CMR 20.05. Under 20.05(1) a pharmacy located in Massachusetts must notify the Board within 14 calendar days of the resignation, termination or change of its Manager of Record, and the change-of-MOR application satisfies that duty. Under 20.05(3) the departing Manager of Record must personally notify the Board of his or her resignation or termination within 14 calendar days, a duty missing from role_duties[4]. The section also omits the report due within 30 days after a transfer of ownership or change of Manager of Record, which compounding pharmacies file under 20.06(6)(e) and non-resident pharmacies under 20.07(2).
findings.rationale: Each sentence is hedged to 247 CMR 6.10 or 6.00, so each is literally true, but the declared subtopic is which changes need notice 'on what clock'. The framing leaves a candidate believing a change of MOR carries no deadline. On Massachusetts facts the pharmacy must notify the Board within 14 calendar days of the change, a duty that a change-of-MOR application filed in that window satisfies. The outgoing MOR owes a separate personal notice on the same clock. The timing table, the retrieval drill and the outgoing-MOR duty therefore teach an incomplete answer, and the drill teaches a wrong one, on a testable number. The 'prior approval' label is also inexact. 6.10(1) requires an application for approval 'whenever there is a change' and contains no bar on the change taking effect first; the MOR may already have died or been terminated. 20.05 treats that same application as the post-event notice. This also fails actor_and_scope, because the outgoing MOR's own duty is missing, and study_usefulness_without_legal_distortion.

findings.problem: 247 CMR 6.11(1) directs the outgoing licensee to comply with 247 CMR 6.12 and 6.13 'pertaining to closing a pharmacy and distributing controlled substances'. The section restates this as '247 CMR 6.12 and 247 CMR 6.13, the notification and closing provisions', which replaces the regulation's own description and drops its controlled-substance distribution limb. The section never says that the seller's stock moves under 247 CMR 6.14, although that section is headed Distribution of Controlled Substances upon Closure or Transfer of Ownership and 6.11(3)(c) invokes its inventory. 6.14 requires certified notice to the Board with the eight 6.14(1) particulars at least 14 days before the CS transfer, and no transfer sooner than 14 days after that notice. On the transfer date the transferor takes an inventory of Schedules II-V and PMP-reportable Schedule VI, signed by both Managers of Record. Both pharmacies file an attestation within ten days, and the transferor may not possess any controlled substances after the transfer date. Two statements are incomplete as a result: orientation[2] calls a transfer 'the one change that generates two independent duties on the same clock', and decision_logic[2] lists only the two 6.11 filings.
findings.rationale: The cross-reference numbers in 6.11(1) do not match its descriptive words: 6.12 is the name-change notice, and CS distribution is 6.14. A faithful paraphrase would keep the words and flag the mismatch. Resolving it silently in favour of 'notification' removes exactly the controlled-substance handling that orientation[3] calls the thing the Board protects when a pharmacy changes hands. It also departs from the section's own dependency record for MA-PHARMACY-OWNERSHIP-TRANSFER, which says the outgoing licensee must comply with the controlled substance distribution provisions. On Massachusetts sale facts a candidate would miss the seller's 6.14 notice, waiting period, dual-signed inventory, ten-day attestation and possession bar. This also fails actor_and_scope, because the outgoing licensee's duties are understated, and decision_logic, through decision_logic[2].

findings.problem: The section says federal law 'enters only as a reference point inside the suitability inquiry' and that the controlled-substance paperwork is 'Board-facing rather than a federal filing'. Both statements mislead. Inside 247 CMR itself, 6.11(1) sends the outgoing licensee to the closing provisions, and 6.13(6)(b) requires an attestation that the stock was disposed of under a federal disposal regulation, or transferred in accordance with 21 CFR 1301.52 and 247 CMR 6.14. Independently of 247 CMR, the same events carry DEA steps a candidate needs. A DEA registration cannot be assigned or transferred without DEA's written consent (21 CFR 1301.52(b)), so a buyer needs its own registration. A registrant transferring its business together with its controlled substances must give the DEA Special Agent in Charge at least 14 days' advance notice, in person or by registered or certified mail, unless the Special Agent in Charge waives the period. It must also take a complete inventory on the transfer date, which serves as both the final and the initial inventory, and move Schedule I and II stock on order forms (1301.52(d) and (e)). A change of name or address is made by a written request to modify the DEA registration (1301.51(a)).
findings.rationale: The MPJE tests federal and Massachusetts law together, and the sale or relocation of a pharmacy is a standard DEA question. An ma_vs_federal field that says federal law plays no role outside suitability would lead a candidate applying the section to a Massachusetts sale or move to leave out the DEA notice, the new registration and the address modification. The Board-facing framing is right for the Massachusetts controlled substance registration, which the Board issues (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7; 247 CMR 2.00; 247 CMR 6.04(2)(c)). It must not be presented as the whole controlled-substance picture. This also fails unsupported_propositions, because the 'only' claim is not supported.

findings.problem: The section lists sterile, complex non-sterile, institutional sterile and non-resident sterile compounding pharmacies as covered by 6.15(1). It then presents the 6.15(3) submissions as the whole remodel filing: the layout, prescription-area and counseling-area drawings, the CS transport plan, and any other information. It omits 6.15(4), under which those four compounding types must also submit certified blueprints of the compounding areas showing the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control and any containment hoods. They must also submit a containment strategy, an environmental monitoring plan, a plan to re-certify the engineering controls and containment hoods, and a continuity-of-care plan, as applicable. The section also omits 6.15(2): sterile, non-resident sterile and institutional sterile compounding pharmacies must apply for approval before moving, adding, modifying, removing or replacing any secondary engineering control, and may not do so until approved. That is a separate express bar, and the teaching that exactly two changes carry an express prohibition (learning_objectives[2], retrieval_prompts[3]) leaves it out. A minor point: by its terms the 6.15(3) list attaches to an application to change the configuration or square footage, while the section labels it the remodeling list.
findings.rationale: The declared learning objective is to 'List what each application must carry', and the section itself brings the compounding types within its remodel scope. Applied to a Massachusetts sterile compounding pharmacy reconfiguring its cleanroom, the section's checklist would miss the five specific 6.15(4) submissions and the prohibition on changing secondary engineering controls. This also fails overgeneralization, because the 6.15(3) list is presented as universal, and decision_logic, through decision_logic[5].

findings.problem: decision_logic[7] tells the candidate to reach for the 247 CMR 6.03 factors whenever a question asks what the Board may do with an application. The change of Manager of Record is one of the applications the section teaches, and there the Board's discretion runs under 247 CMR 6.10(3). That subsection has its own ten factors aimed at the proposed Manager of Record. It adds discipline by the Board within five years of the application (6.10(3)(h)), and it does not include the 6.03 factors for prescriptive privileges (6.03(9)) or for assuming ownership to circumvent 247 CMR 2.00 (6.03(3)). The section never mentions 6.10(3), although it describes the change-of-MOR application in detail and notes that the Board may approve or deny it.
findings.rationale: A candidate asked on what grounds the Board may refuse a change-of-MOR application would be sent to the wrong list. That candidate might treat prescriptive privileges as a listed ground, or miss the five-year Board-discipline factor. The rule should be limited to new-licence and transfer-of-ownership applications (6.03, 6.04(5), 6.11(4)), and 6.10(3) should be taught for the MOR change. This also fails decision_logic.

findings.problem: MA-Q-0361 is a select-all question that keys choice D as correct: prior discipline on a separate professional licence is a listed suitability factor. The section never mentions 247 CMR 6.03(10) or (11), the discipline of, or a disciplinary consent agreement on, the person's own professional licence or registration. Its 'Whose history counts?' row describes the history that counts as conduct at a pharmacy, health care facility or FDA- or DEA-registered entity that the person owned, operated or held an interest in. If anything, that steers a candidate away from D.
findings.rationale: A released question mapped to the section must be answerable from it. A candidate relying on the section would select A and E, miss D, and get MA-Q-0361 wrong. Nothing in the section contradicts the key, but D cannot be supported from it. Adding 6.03(10) and (11) to comparison_tables[2] would close the gap. The other four mapped questions (MA-Q-0362, 0386, 0387, 0390) are answerable and consistent.

results.summary: MAJOR_REWRITE, severity High. The section's core propositions are accurate against the current 247 CMR 6.00 text, and I verified each. Name change: written notice within 14 days with authorizing documentation (6.12, which reaches only the operating name). Transfer of ownership: the licensee's notice and the proposed new licensee's application, each at least 14 days before the transfer; the incoming application items in 6.11(3); and the 6.03 screen of the new licensee and interest holders (6.11(4)). Relocation: application at least 90 days ahead unless the Board approves otherwise, and a bar on relocating before approval (6.16). Remodel: a bar on starting work before approval, with the 6.15(3) items. Change of Manager of Record: the dual-signed inventory attestation reaching reportable Schedule VI, the death/serious illness/termination substitution with notice of the reason, and the original licence and fees (6.10(2)). Suitability: the eleven 6.03 factors framed as reaching applicant, licensee or interest holder, counting FDA/DEA-registered entity history, and including prescriptive privileges. The licence-does-not-pass point is consistent with 6.04(8). The section nonetheless fails its own declared subtopic ('which need notice, on what clock') in several places. It teaches the change of Manager of Record as having no clock, when 247 CMR 20.05 requires notice within 14 calendar days of the change and a separate 14-day personal notice from the departing MOR (High). Its paraphrase of 6.11(1) drops the controlled-substance distribution limb, so the seller's 6.14 duties on a sale never appear (Medium). Its ma_vs_federal field wrongly says federal law enters only through suitability, which hides the 21 CFR 1301.52 transfer-of-business and non-assignability rules and the 1301.51 name and address modification (Medium). It presents the 6.15(3) list as the whole remodel filing for compounding pharmacies, omitting 6.15(4) and the 6.15(2) secondary-engineering-control bar (Medium). Its decision rule sends every Board-discretion question to 6.03, although the change-of-MOR application is screened under 6.10(3) (Medium). It cannot support the keyed choice D of mapped question MA-Q-0361 (Medium). The repairs touch about 25 locations, including the timing taxonomy, the transfer-of-ownership narrative and the whole ma_vs_federal field, so this needs rewriting rather than touch-ups. Not publishable as it stands.

findings.problem: The prompt asks 'Which pharmacies must identify a continuity-of-care pharmacy'. The answer lists sterile compounding, complex non-sterile compounding, institutional sterile compounding, non-resident sterile compounding and non-resident complex non-sterile compounding pharmacies. 247 CMR 6.13(7) states that 6.13(3) is not required for institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, so a correct answer leaves them out.
findings.rationale: The answer key copies the 6.13(3) list without the 6.13(7) subtraction. It therefore drills the wrong result on exactly the type-specific carve-out that the section itself calls the easiest point to get wrong. It contradicts the section's own comparison_tables[1].rows[4], worked_examples[1] and retrieval_prompts[7]. As a stand-alone flashcard it teaches that an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy must name a continuity-of-care pharmacy, which is wrong law. This also fails study_usefulness_without_legal_distortion.

findings.problem: The row describes the 6.14(2)(d) transfer attestation as 'separate from, and later than, the closure attestation under 6.13(6)(b)'. Neither provision orders the two filings. The transfer attestation is due within ten days of the transfer. The closure attestation is due within 14 days of closure and must certify that the stock has already been transferred. When the stock moves on or before the closure date, the ten-day attestation will ordinarily fall due first.
findings.rationale: 'Separate' is correct, but 'later than' is a sequencing claim the regulation does not support. It could mislead a candidate asked which filing comes first. Low, because the two deadlines are stated correctly elsewhere (comparison_tables[3].rows[2], timing_deadlines[5] and [7]).

findings.problem: Notice goes on day 1 and the premature move is on day 10. On the scenario's own day numbering, an attestation filed 'on day 20 counting from the notice' falls ten days after the transfer, which is within the 6.14(2)(d) window. The resolution still counts the day-20 plan as one of 'three separate errors', saying it carries the 14-day figure onto the ten-day duty.
findings.rationale: steps[3] states the rule correctly: ten days from the transfer, not from the notice. But the facts do not produce the late filing the resolution claims, or do so only on a strained reading of 'counting from the notice'. A candidate who checks the arithmetic learns either that the example is wrong or that a timely filing was late. The example should use facts where a notice-based count actually misses the ten-day window.

findings.problem: The section rightly says the 6.13(6)(b) attestation certifies disposal under the federal disposal regulation, or transfer 'in accordance with 21 CFR 1301.52 and 247 CMR 6.14'. It never says what the federal side requires, and its action list for moving the stock (decision_logic[6]) holds only the Board-facing 6.14 steps. Under 21 CFR 1301.52, a registrant transferring its business with its controlled substances gives the DEA Special Agent in Charge at least 14 days' advance notice, in person or by registered or certified mail, unless the Special Agent in Charge waives the period. It takes a transfer-date inventory that serves as the final and initial inventory, moves Schedule I and II stock on order forms, and passes the records to the transferee. A registrant that discontinues without a transfer returns its DEA certificate and unexecuted order forms for cancellation, and may dispose of its stock under Part 1317. The disposal section that 6.13(6)(b) cites, 21 CFR 1307.21, no longer appears in the CFR; registrant disposal is now governed by 21 CFR 1317.05. The section's phrase 'the federal disposal regulation it cites' leaves this unexplained. It also never distinguishes the Board-issued controlled substances registration, which goes back to the Board, from the DEA registration, which goes back to DEA.
findings.rationale: Nothing the section states is wrong, and its declared scope is the Massachusetts procedure, hence Low. But the attestation it teaches certifies federal compliance. A candidate following its action list could sign that attestation without having taken the DEA steps the attestation vouches for.

results.summary: MINOR_EDIT, severity Medium. The section is accurate and thorough on nearly every proposition, and I checked it line by line against the current 247 CMR 6.13 and 6.14. Closure notice (6.13(1)): certified written notice at least 14 days ahead unless the Board authorizes otherwise, with the six particulars. Non-resident notice (6.13(2)): the four particulars, dropping the CS registration number, the MOR's name and the CS procedures. Continuity of care (6.13(3)): the type list, certified mail and the Board override. Patients (6.13(4)): the 90-day look-back, the 14-day attempted notice by first class mail or other Board approved method with no Board-override qualifier, the conspicuous posted notice, and the non-resident duty to notify all Massachusetts patients. Patient files (6.13(5)): transfer on request or as law or contract requires. Post-closure (6.13(6)): the 14-day submission and attestation, which does not apply to non-resident pharmacies. Carve-out (6.13(7)): it names only (3) and (4). CS transfer (6.14): the eight particulars, the 14-day wait, the transfer-date inventory including reportable Schedule VI, the dual MOR signatures with the staff-pharmacist substitution, two-year readily retrievable retention, the ten-day attestation by both pharmacies, and the bar on transferor possession. The actors are right throughout. All four mapped questions (MA-Q-0072, 0074, 0363, 0385) are answerable and consistent. Blocking defect: the retrieval_prompts[6] answer key lists institutional sterile compounding pharmacies among those that must name a continuity-of-care pharmacy, contrary to 6.13(7) (Medium). Low: 'later than' in comparison_tables[2].rows[4] is unsupported sequencing; the arithmetic of worked_examples[2] does not demonstrate the attestation error it claims; and the federal steps that the attestation certifies under 21 CFR 1301.52, the superseded 1307.21 citation (now 21 CFR 1317.05) and the CSR/DEA-registration distinction are left unexplained. Points I considered and did not treat as defects: calling the 6.14 transferee 'Board-licensed' where 6.14(1) says 'another licensed pharmacy' is supported contextually by the 6.14(1)(d) and (f) particulars, since 247 CMR 2.00 defines the controlled substance registration as Board-issued and the Manager of Record as Board-registered. Assigning the pharmacies' 6.14 duties to the Managers of Record in role_duties[6] and [7] is consistent with the 2.00 definition of the MOR as responsible for operating the pharmacy in conformance with the law.
